content.summary_of_the_paper: The goal of this paper is to understand what “knowledge’’ is transferred in knowledge distillation (KD). The main finding is that in logit-based, feature-based, and contrastive knowledge distillation, often a student becomes similar to its teacher in some unexpected ways. In particular, with experiments on ImageNet the paper demonstrates that there is noticeable transfer of object localizations, invariances to data transformations, performance on unseen (for the student) domains, texture/shape biases, and adversarial vulnerability.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Overall, this is a well-rounded submission towards understanding knowledge distillation, which is an important topic for the ICLR community. The paper is well-written; experiments are done with care, making sure that the observed effects are not artifacts of distillation; the main experimental findings are convincing; details for reproducing the work are presented; and related work is adequately cited. To my best knowledge the observations are novel.

Nevertheless, there are some aspects that can be improved.

1. The main question “what knowledge is being transferred in KD” remains largely not formalized and unanswered. What this submission does is to reveal disconnected cases where a student becomes similar to its teacher in some aspect. The choice of these aspects is not well-motivated and principled. Are there any principled notions of “knowledge” whose transfer can explain the observations of this paper? What are the connections between the various “types” of knowledge? Addressing these questions is not trivial, but can be a great addition to this submission.

2. The effect of knowledge distillation is not as strong on ImageNet as on other commonly considered datasets, such as CIFAR-100. Many works observed challenges in making KD work on ImageNet (see for example [1]). In this sense studying knowledge distillation with only experiments on ImageNet does not provide a holistic view. I recommend adding some experiments on CIFAR-100.

3. Sec. 5 introduces a hypothesis that mimicking the teacher at a particular layer not only makes the student’s representation at the corresponding layer similar, but also results in similar representations in layers right before the corresponding teacher and student layers. There are many issues with this section.
    * The hypothesis is not well-supported, as there are not enough experiments and it is hard to judge how significant are minor CKA score changes (for example from 0.86 to 0.91).
    * Is the goal of this section to explain the observed phenomena? I do not see how can this provide a strong explanation on how *contrastive* knowledge distillation can transfer adversarial vulnerability and how the three considered KD methods can transfer performance on unseen domains or data transformations.
    * It seems that the function matching perspective of Beyer et al. [2] is a good candidate for explaining why knowledge distillation results in transfer of various notions of knowledge. I recommend checking whether better matching of teacher and student functions results in better transfer of the considered notions of knowledge. This can be done as in Beyer et al. [2] by using consistent data augmentations, using mixup, and training the student longer.



### Minor comments

1. Sec 4.5 “Other studies” should shortly summarize the findings of the additional experiments presented in the appendix.

2. In Section 6.1, the paper shows that sometimes knowledge distillation can transfer performance on unseen (for the student) domains on which the teacher was trained. Using MNIST-based datasets to support this is not desirable. Due to its simplicity it is hard to judge whether similar observations will hold for other datasets.

3. Cosine similarity for class activation maps might not be a good way to measure similarity, as it accounts for possibly large regions that are not relevant in any way.

4. When reading the paper I had the impression that there is a hidden assumption that KD works because there is a transfer of some kind of tangible notion of knowledge. Will this explain the performance of self-distillation? The paper should do more justice to existing works that explain the success of KD from other perspectives, such as optimization and regularization (for example works like [3] and [4]).

### References

[1] Jang Hyun Cho and Bharath Hariharan. On the efficacy of knowledge distillation. In ICCV, 2019.

[2] Lucas Beyer, Xiaohua Zhai, Amelie Royer, Larisa Markeeva, Rohan Anil, and Alexander Kolesnikov. ´ Knowledge distillation: A good teacher is patient and consistent. In CVPR, 2022.

[3] Mary Phuong and Christoph Lampert. Towards understanding knowledge distillation. In ICML, 2019.

[4] Hossein Mobahi, Mehrdad Farajtabar, and Peter Bartlett. Self-distillation amplifies regularization in Hilbert space. In NeurIPS, 2020.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, this submission is a significant first step towards understanding what is being transferred in knowledge distillation and the mechanisms behind this transfer. The weaknesses listed above are not critical in my opinion, but addressing them will improve the submission greatly. I am willing to increase the score in that case.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper aims to understand what information gets distilled to the student from the teacher in knowledge distillation. In order to understand this, the authors set up multiple experiments to understand the student performance and compared to an independent model under each scenario, including localization, adversarial vulnerability, invariance to data transformations, and unseen domain knowledge. The authors also tried to understand why the student gets these information despite not specifically training on them, and pointed out their practical implications.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The paper is well written and easy to follow. The logic of the paper is clear. The authors broke down the big question of understanding knowledge distillation into several concrete directions, and set up corresponding experiments. The experiment results look very consistent. The authors also tried to provide an explanation for the observations, and designed experiments to justify their hypothesis. 

Weakness:
While Sec 5 tries to provide an explanation for their experiment observations, it would be good to go further and understand why this layer-wise similarity happens. E.g., in KL or CRD, the student learns most from the teacher of the last layer output. Does the back propagation process leads to the similarity of each layer? This should provide some deeper understanding and maybe theoretical analysis on how much the knowledge can be distilled for KL or CRD, etc.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written, with clear logic to understand the proposed question about knowledge distillation. While there are some work done before to understand what knowledge are distilled during knowledge distillation, this paper provides a more systematic analysis. The analysis is done using published methods and datasets, and should be reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is clear written. The authors performed multiple experiments for each analysis, and proposed their hypothesis for the experiment observations. They also performed additional experiments to validate their hypothesis. It would be great to have some deeper understanding of the proposed hypothesis, e.g. why this happens and how, but it could be another more theoretical work.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper aims to understand knowledge distillation through three types of KD approaches: (1) logits distillation via KL-divergence; (2) feature distillation of hint (FitNets); (3) contrastive representation distillation.

The core problem studied in this paper is “what is the knowledge that gets distilled in knowledge distillation? i.e., in what ways does the student become similar to the teacher?” This paper attempts to answer the following questions:

    - Does KD start to localize objects in the same way? 

    - Does KD get fooled by the same adversarial samples? 

    - Does KD’s data invariance property become similar?

Extensive experiments are conducted in this paper with multiple configurations of teacher-student architectures, such as ResNet50 → ResNet18, VGG19 → VGG11, etc.,  on ImageNet, MNIST, as well as images from artistic domain datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths:

    - The motivation in this paper of understanding knowledge for distillation technique is interesting and also important for this approach.

    - This paper provided comprehensive experiments on different aspects of learned knowledge, such as localization, fooling adversarial samples, and data invariance properties.

### Weaknesses:

    This is an empirical paper with extensive experiments, but containing limited/no theoretical analysis and explanations. It may be interesting to people who are working on relevant topics but not in a deep or fundamental way to explain the mechanism of KD. My main concern for this paper is that, since this is an empirical work, the main datasets used in this paper seem neither large nor reliable enough, and the used network architectures are still not sufficient, even though the authors have tried to involve more different models, which may cause biased conclusions on the knowledge distillation technique, and further raise more confusions to people.

    The evidence for this concern is that, in this paper, there are many inconsistent behaviors or observations existing with the used backbones and datasets. For example, in section 4.1 of localization experiments, Fig. 2 shows that when ResNet50 → ResNet18, CAM accuracy of KL is better than CRD, however, when using VGG19 → VGG11, the result is the opposite. The corresponding discussion does not explain why and how different architectures affect the results. And more inconsistent results and comparisons also exist in Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 5, Fig. 6, etc.

    These inconsistent phenomena, which are not easy to explain, completely defeat the original intention of this paper, i.e., “Our goal is to shed some light on the dark knowledge.” In contrast, these experiments and observations just make people feel more confused about how knowledge distillation truly works.

    I think it’s better to provide empirical agreements on knowledge distillation, rather than random/diverse empirical observations on it since we have enough phenomena from a mass of literature on KD, but they are often contradictory.

    Moreover, if changing another dataset, I’m afraid the conclusions observed in this paper are hard to hold still. More than one dataset on each exploratory aspect is necessary to guarantee the reliability and solidness of the phenomena and conclusions on KD observed in this paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity and writing quality look good in this paper, the novelty is limited, and the paper provides enough details for reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: This is an empirical paper aiming to understand knowledge distillation. The paper provided many experiments on localization, fooling adversarial samples, data invariance properties, etc. However, it’s hard to evaluate whether the value of these observations is significant, and I feel these observations may even play negative effects for people to understand KD since many inconsistencies exist among them. More than one dataset on every single ablation is undoubtedly necessary to verify the consistency of the phenomena and conclusions derived from this paper in a more solid way.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Sufficient experiments on three well-known knowledge distillation methods have been conducted.
2. It's interesting to study the behaviour of students and teachers in knowledge distillation. 
3. Good paper writing.

Weakness:
1. Only experimental studies are provided and there is no theoretical analysis. There is no enough discussion to explain what they have found. 
2. Many of these results, e.g. CAM, Agreement, CKA have already been utilized to analysis the performance of students and teachers in previous works.
3. Most of the conclusions in this paper are naive and very intuitive. To be honset, I did not find any take-aways from this paper.

content.title: Response to the reviewers
content.comment: We thank reviewers dM3q, mYQA, and biiJ for their constructive comments. We will try to incorporate the suggestions in our future revision. Unfortunately, we think reviewer Fxbn has not offered any valuable suggestions, and has not given sufficient attention that a submission deserves. We are disappointed at the level of unprofessionalism displayed by Fxbn. At this time, even though we can address the concerns raised by most of the reviewers, we are choosing to withdraw and submit to a different venue.
